ety.text: From earlier barbetter (“to dig about”), from Middle French borbeter (“to shake in the mud”), of uncertain origin:. * Possibly from barbe (“beard”) + -oter * From bourbouter (“wading (in mud)”), from bourbe (“mud, mire”) * From an onomatopoeic root influenced by Latin ballus, from Ancient Greek βαλλίζω (ballízō, “to jump about”); this is also found in the second element of the genus Zygoballus * Less likely, related to the fish barbote

ety.text: Literally "to play the harp." A pun on harpe (“harp”), which is also slang for "finger," and harper (“slang, to steal”), as well as an allusion to the digital dexterity needed to pick pockets, compared to that of playing the harp. Compare English fiddle (“slang, to mess with; to fraudulently manipulate”) and obsolete finger (“to steal, purloin”).
